I prefer spirit-forward sipping drinks to the more diluted juice or mixer cocktails, so I generally go with an Old-Fashioned or a Caipirinha, the latter of which is unbeatable on a hot day. For either of these recipes you need at least a half-decent spirit look for some things at least in the $20-$25 range. Some people prefer to shake the Caipirinha, but I tend to go with it stirred as it will be a little less bitter from the lime rind.

Note that both of these should be sipped and enjoyed, if you drink them fast you'll have a bad time.

 

Old Fashioned:

Ingredients: Bourbon (2oz), Brown Suger (1 tbsp), Bitters (Angora - 2 to 3 dashes), Water (1 dash), Ice

Tools: Mixer, Muddler, Rocks Glass

How I make it

  • Take rocks glass and muddle a tablespoon of brown sugar, the bitters and a splash of water until the sugar is fully dissolved. You should end up with a thick syrupy mix, not a fast flowing liquid.
  • Tilt and rotate the glass to coat the sides of the glass in the syrup.
  • Place 3-4 cubes of ice in the glass
  • Pour Bourbon over the ice and stir gently

Cairpirinha

Ingredients: White/SIlver Rum (2 oz), Limes (at least 1/2 per drink), White Sugar (1 tbsp), Ice

Tools: Mixer, Muddler, Rocks Glass

How I make it

  • Cut the lime into 1/8 wedges.
  • Place 3/8 of lime and a tablespoon of sugar into the bottom of the rocks glass
  • Muddle vigorously, you want to get all of the juice of the lime extracted as well as some of the bitterness of the peel - all of the sugar needs to be dissolved.
  • Put 3-4 cubes of ice in the glass
  • Pour rum into the glass and stir
  • Garnish with the 4th lime wedge.
Isn't the caipirinha just a daiquiri with lime wedges in it? I thought you needed a certain type of spirit from Brazil.

They're similar only in ingredients, the preparation is different. Caipirinhas start by muddling the lime with the sugar to get the juices and oils out. Daiquiris just mix (stir or shake) lime juice and simple syrup with the spirit.

And yes, Caipirinhas use Cachaça aka "Brazilian Rum".

Your second drink is actually a Caipirissima.

A Caipirinha actually uses Cachaça (sometimes referred to as "Brazilian Rum"). Like rum, it is similarly distilled from sugarcane juice, although rum is typically made from molasses. It definitely has a more distinctive taste than your run-of-the-mill rum.

Interesting, I always just considered Chachaca as a form of Rum with a distinct taste. I didn't know it was technically a different liquor, or that the drink I was making was a different name when I wasn't making it with that. Thanks for the info!

You're welcome!

In the US, Cachaça was classified as rum until recently. They're both under the "sugercane spirit" umbrella, and I'd consider them more siblings than parent-child.

If anything cachaça is more similar to rhum agricole (a french-carribean spirit, also distilled from fresh-pressed sugarcane juice), albeit usually at a much higher proof (cachaça: 76-96 proof vs rhum agricole 80-140 proof).

Summer months, I make pineapple-infused tequila. Buy a fresh, ripe pineapple. Peel and core the pineapple, and cut into moderate-sized pieces. Put the pineapple on a hot grill, and cook until the pineapple is getting nice grill marks and is browning slightly. Throw the pineapple chunks into a large glass jar (like you're use to make sun tea) and add a fifth of decent quality (no Cuervo) silver tequila. Let it sit for a minimum of two days. Use tongs to remove the pineapple chunks. Put a coffee filter in a funnel and pour the remaining liquid through, back into the original tequila bottle. You can gently press the pineapple chunks to express a bit of extra fluid and save it as well. The resulting liquid is divine ambrosia. Use carefully.
